items.prompt: More than thirty stalls sell wood carvings at the Katutura curio market, buyers walk freely between them, and each stall charges close to the going price. Define a competitive market as the term applies to this curio market.
items.canonical_answer: A competitive market has many buyers and sellers, and each seller is too small to influence the market price. Here, more than thirty stalls sell similar carvings and buyers move freely between them, so no single stall can raise the going price.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a high number of sellers, each too small to influence the market price set by the whole market's demand and supply.
The meaning must rest on the market's structure - many small sellers and free switching - not on any claim that prices in such markets are low by definition.

items.prompt: Braai-wood sellers at Swakopmund's open market sell 3 600 bundles a month at N$30 a bundle. Four new sellers set up stalls, and the market settles at 3 900 bundles a month at N$28 a bundle. Discuss how the entry of the new sellers is linked to the change in price and quantity, and the likely consequences for buyers and for the sellers already trading.
items.canonical_answer: The four new sellers add stalls, so more bundles are offered at each price, while buyers' wishes have not changed. At the old price of N$30, sellers now offer more bundles than buyers want, so stalls are likely to cut prices to sell their wood. Because buyers walk freely between stalls, a seller who stays at N$30 tends to lose customers to cheaper neighbours. The price falls by N$30 - N$28 = N$2, and at the lower price buyers take more, so sales rise by 3 900 - 3 600 = 300 bundles a month. Buyers gain a lower price and more stalls to choose from. Existing sellers get N$2 less a bundle and share the market with more stalls, so their profit per bundle is likely to narrow. How far this goes depends on whether selling braai-wood at N$28 still covers sellers' costs: if it does, more sellers may enter and the price may fall further; if not, some stalls may leave.
marking_guidance: The link: the answer must connect the entry of four sellers to more bundles offered at each price, and explain how buyers switching freely between stalls puts downward pressure on the N$30 price.

The consequence: the N$2 fall to N$28 and the 300 extra bundles a month must be calculated, and the consequence named for each party - buyers paying less with more stalls to choose from, existing sellers facing a lower price and a thinner margin.
Discussion: an 8-mark answer reaches a view on how far the effect goes - whether N$28 still covers sellers' costs, so that entry continues or some stalls leave.

items.prompt:
Table 1 - two taxi ranks, 2026
Oshakati rank: 14 operators, average fare N$25 a trip
Otavi rank: 3 operators, average fare N$35 a trip
Explain what the figures suggest about the effect of the number of sellers on the price in these two taxi markets.
items.canonical_answer: The figures suggest that more sellers go with a lower price: Oshakati's rank has 14 operators and an average fare of N$25, while Otavi's has 3 operators and charges N$35, which is N$35 - N$25 = N$10 more. With many operators, each is too small to raise the fare alone, because passengers can move to the next taxi. With only three, each has more control and passengers have fewer choices. However, route lengths and costs may also differ, so the figures suggest the effect but do not prove it.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the inverse relationship between operator numbers and the average fare - must be stated first.
Supporting evidence: the comparison across the two ranks, with the N$10 gap attached, must back the statement.

Why: an explanation of the relationship - each seller too small to influence the price where sellers are many, and fewer alternatives where sellers are few - is the core mark; quoting the fares alone is not interpretation.
The exception earns its mark: however, cost differences between the ranks may explain part of the gap.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells bottled juice at the Opuwo open market, where four other juice sellers trade. The going price is N$12 a bottle, and Kaoko Juice fills about 900 bottles a month at that price. Its manager considers charging N$15 a bottle. Explain, using the context of this market, why Kaoko Juice is likely to lose sales if it lifts its price above the going level.
items.canonical_answer: Kaoko Juice is one of five small sellers of similar juice, and buyers move freely between stalls. The N$12 price is set by demand and supply across the whole market, not by one seller. If Kaoko charges N$15 while rivals charge N$12, buyers can save N$15 - N$12 = N$3 a bottle by going elsewhere, so its sales are likely to fall below 900 bottles a month. Therefore it can keep its customers only by charging close to the going price.
marking_guidance: The context - five sellers, the N$12 going price, the free switching of buyers - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the price is set across the whole market, the link is the N$3 saving that switches buyers to rivals.
Conclusion: therefore the seller is too small to influence the price and takes the going price as given - that closes the explanation.

items.prompt: Two new salons open at the Katutura hairdressing rank, where twelve salons trade at about N$60 a haircut, each carrying costs of about N$40 a cut. The going price drifts to about N$50. Analyse the consequences of the new sellers entering for clients, the twelve existing salons' owners, and the two new salons' owners.
items.canonical_answer: Two new salons raise the number of sellers from twelve to fourteen, so more haircuts are offered at each price. Because clients move freely between salons, the newcomers attract trade by charging about N$50, and existing salons cut prices to keep clients, so the going price falls from N$60 to N$50. Clients save N$60 - N$50 = N$10 a cut, and some who found N$60 too dear return. Existing salons' profit per cut falls from N$60 - N$40 = N$20 to N$50 - N$40 = N$10. The new salons gain clients but earn the same thinner N$10 margin. So clients gain, while existing owners lose half their margin per cut.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - two new salons entering a market of twelve - must open the analysis.
Mechanism: because clients switch freely, this causes the going price to drift down from N$60 as salons match the newcomers.
Consequence: therefore each named party needs its own traced outcome - the client's N$10 saving, the existing owner's margin halving, the newcomer's volume.
For whom: state for whom each consequence lands - the consumer, the twelve existing firms, the two new firms.

items.prompt: Thirty small furniture workshops trade in Windhoek's northern industrial area, each selling similar chairs close to the going price of N$950, and buyers drive freely between the workshops. New workshops may open on a small council registration fee. Explain the features that make this furniture market a competitive market.
items.canonical_answer: There are many sellers: thirty workshops, none large compared with the whole market. Each is too small to raise the N$950 price on its own, because buyers can easily drive to another workshop. Buyers switch freely between thirty similar suppliers, which keeps prices in check. Entry is easy, since a new workshop needs only a small registration fee, and new entrants help keep the price near the level set by demand and supply across the market.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are a high number of sellers, each too small to influence the market price, easy switching between sellers, and low barriers to entry - each explained in the market's own terms, not merely listed.
What it includes: the going price of N$950 set across the whole market, not by any single workshop, is the fact that carries the second mark.

items.prompt: The council of a riverside town has licensed one operator alone to run the ferry crossing at Katima Mulilo, and travellers who need the crossing have few other ways over the water. Define a monopoly as the term applies to this ferry market.
items.canonical_answer: A monopoly is a market with a single dominant seller protected by barriers to entry, so it sets its own price within what buyers will pay. Here, one licensed operator runs the ferry, the licence keeps rivals out, and travellers have few alternatives.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a single dominant seller behind barriers to entry, setting its own price within what buyers will pay.
The meaning must rest on the market's structure - one protected seller and limited alternatives - not on the seller's size alone.

items.prompt: The fuel station at Ruacana is the only station within 90 km. It raises its price from N$22 to N$25 a litre, and its sales fall from 9 000 litres to 7 200 litres a month. Discuss how the station's position as the single seller is linked to its ability to raise its price, and the consequences of the higher price for its customers and for the station.
items.canonical_answer: The 90 km to the next station is a barrier to entry, so drivers in the area have few alternatives and the station can set its own price. It raised the price by N$25 - N$22 = N$3 a litre and kept most of its sales. Even so, sales fell by 9 000 - 7 200 = 1 800 litres a month, because some drivers make fewer trips, share lifts or buy fuel elsewhere when they can. Customers pay N$3 more on each litre they still buy, and those who cut trips lose some travel. For the station, monthly takings fall from N$22 x 9 000 = N$198 000 to N$25 x 7 200 = N$180 000, but it also buys 1 800 fewer litres from its supplier, so whether it gains depends on its cost per litre. A single seller can choose its price, but buyers still respond to it; the barrier means it loses some sales rather than most of them.
marking_guidance: The link: the answer must connect the 90 km barrier and the lack of nearby alternatives to the station's ability to raise its price without losing most of its sales.

The consequence: the N$3 rise and the 1 800-litre fall must be calculated, with the consequence named for customers (paying more per litre, travelling less) and for the station (higher price, fewer litres sold, takings falling from N$198 000 to N$180 000).
Discussion: an 8-mark answer reaches a view - whether the station gains depends on its cost per litre, and a single seller still faces buyers who respond to its price.

items.prompt:
Etosha Gate Lodge, the only lodge at its gate, records two seasons.
Season 1: room price N$900 a night, 2 520 room-nights sold
Season 2: room price N$1 200 a night, 1 960 room-nights sold
Explain what the figures show about the demand the lodge faces as the single seller at the gate.
items.canonical_answer: When the lodge raised its price from N$900 to N$1 200 a night, room-nights sold fell by 2 520 - 1 960 = 560. This shows it faces a downward-sloping demand curve: as the only lodge at the gate it can set its price, but at a higher price some travellers stay elsewhere, stay fewer nights or skip the trip. However, the seasons may differ in holidays, wildlife or visitor numbers, so part of the fall may not be caused by the N$1 200 - N$900 = N$300 rise.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the negative relationship between the lodge's price and the room-nights sold - must be stated first.
Supporting evidence: the comparison across the two seasons, with the 560-room-night fall attached, must back the statement.
Why: an explanation of the relationship - the downward-sloping demand curve a single seller faces - is the core mark; quoting the room-nights alone is not interpretation.
The exception earns its mark: however, season differences may explain part of the fall.

items.prompt: Otavi Water Works holds the district's single water licence, households cannot easily switch suppliers, and its monthly household charge is N$180. A survey estimates that several competing suppliers in the same district would tend to charge nearer N$140 a month. Explain, using the context of this market, why the works can hold its charge above that level.
items.canonical_answer: Otavi Water Works has the only water licence, and households cannot easily switch suppliers. It charges N$180 a month, N$180 - N$140 = N$40 more than competing suppliers would be expected to charge. The licence, and the high cost of laying a second set of pipes, keep rivals out. Because households cannot leave for a cheaper supplier, the usual check on price is missing. Therefore the barriers protecting the single seller let the works hold its charge above the many-seller level.
marking_guidance: The context - the single licence, the N$180 charge against the estimated N$140, households unable to switch - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the barriers keep rivals out, the link is the missing check of buyers leaving for a cheaper rival.
Conclusion: therefore the charge sits above the many-seller level - that closes the explanation.

items.prompt: Four minibus operators ran the Gobabis station rank, with fares at N$15 a trip. The council now grants the rank's single operating licence to one operator, who raises the fare to N$22 a trip. Analyse the consequences of the single licence for commuters, the licence holder, and the three operators who lost their permits.
items.canonical_answer: The council's single licence cuts the number of operators from four to one and creates a barrier to entry. Because commuters cannot switch operators and newcomers are kept out, the licence holder no longer faces rivals, so it raises the fare from N$15 to N$22. Commuters pay N$22 - N$15 = N$7 more per trip, so some make fewer trips, share rides or walk. The licence holder earns more on each trip, although it may carry fewer passengers. The three former operators lose their income from the rank and cannot return. So the licence holder gains, while commuters and the former operators lose.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the council granting a single licence, cutting the sellers from four to one - must open the analysis.
Mechanism: because switching is limited and newcomers are kept out, this causes the fare to rise from N$15 to N$22.
Consequence: therefore each named party needs its own traced outcome - the commuter's N$7, the holder's wider margin, the former operators' lost income.
For whom: state for whom each consequence lands - the consumer who rides the route, the licence holder, the three former operators.

items.prompt: Oshakati Maize Mills is the district's single large mill; farmers within 60 km have their maize ground there, and building a second mill of that size is estimated at N$8 million, far more than a newcomer could recover quickly. Explain the features that make this milling market a monopoly.
items.canonical_answer: Oshakati Maize Mills is the single dominant seller, the only large mill within reach of the district's farmers. Building a second mill would cost about N$8 million, a barrier that keeps most new mills out. The mill can set its own grinding fee within what farmers will pay, because those who cannot mill at home must pay it or travel more than 60 km. Farmers have few alternatives, which lets the fee stay above the level several competing mills would charge.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are a single dominant seller, barriers to entry, price-setting within what buyers will pay, and limited alternatives - each explained in the mill's own terms, not merely listed.
What it includes: the N$8 million set-up cost named as the barrier is the fact that carries the second mark.

items.prompt: Explain why a high number of firms in a market tends to keep the quality of products up.
items.canonical_answer: Where many firms sell similar products, buyers can switch easily to a nearby rival. A seller whose quality slips - a salon giving poor haircuts, a stall selling stale bread - tends to lose customers to rivals whose quality is better, and so loses revenue. Because each seller knows this, it has a strong reason to keep its quality up, or to improve it to win customers from others. Therefore rivalry among many sellers tends to hold quality up for buyers.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must explain because buyers can switch freely between many sellers, a seller whose quality slips tends to lose customers and revenue.
Why: the answer must link that threat to each seller's reason to keep quality up, which is how a high number of firms protects buyers.

items.prompt: Kavango Power Distribution holds the single licence to supply electricity in its region and earns a high profit. Analyse the possible advantages of this monopoly for its customers.
items.canonical_answer: As the single supplier, the firm runs one network of lines instead of several rivals duplicating them, so the region avoids paying for wasteful duplicate networks. Its large scale may lower its cost per unit of electricity, and part of the saving may reach customers through lower charges. Its high profit, protected by the licence, may fund research and investment, such as smart meters or solar plants, because no rival can take its customers before the spending pays back. Customers may therefore gain a steadier supply and better service, provided the firm chooses to pass savings on and to invest rather than keep the profit.
marking_guidance: Benefit: the advantage must be named - one network rather than duplicated ones, lower cost per unit from scale, and profit funding research and investment.
Because: each advantage must be developed through its mechanism, so that it leads to lower charges, steadier supply or better service, with the condition that savings are passed on.
For whom: the advantages must be stated for the customers, the party the question names.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. A competitive market is best described as a market in which:
A  the largest seller sets the price for the rest
B  many sellers each hold too small a share to influence the market price
C  the government sets each price
D  two or three large sellers agree the price

2. When new sellers enter a competitive market, the quantity offered at each price rises, and the market price tends to:
A  rise
B  stay fixed by law
C  fall
D  lose all meaning

3. For buyers, the effect of a high number of sellers on choice tends to be:
A  a narrower choice
B  a wider choice
C  no change in choice
D  a single standard product

4. A seller earning unusually high profit in a competitive market is likely to find that over time:
A  new sellers enter and the profit narrows
B  the profit is protected by the market
C  buyers must accept a higher price
D  the seller can raise its price freely

5. A monopoly is best described as:
A  a market with a single dominant seller behind barriers to entry
B  any large firm
C  a market with a few medium-sized sellers
D  a market where the government fixes the price

6. Which of these is a barrier to entry?
A  a government licence that keeps other sellers out
B  a wide choice of products on sale
C  a fall in demand for the good
D  a rise in households' incomes

7. A dominant seller that raises its price tends to find that:
A  the quantity buyers take rises
B  the quantity buyers take falls, as some respond
C  its demand curve shifts to the right
D  buyers' incomes rise to meet the price

8. Which of these may be an advantage for buyers of a single large supplier?
A  its larger scale may lower its cost per unit, and part of the saving may reach the price
B  it can safely ignore its customers
C  it must charge the highest price buyers could pay
D  buyers end up with fewer alternatives
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 B, 4 A, 5 A, 6 A, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B is the definition - many sellers, each too small to influence the price set across the market. A describes a dominant seller's power, not a competitive market; C confuses a competitive market with a planned economy; D describes sellers agreeing prices, which rivalry rules out.
2. C: more sellers offering the good at each price puts downward pressure on the market price. A reverses the direction of entry; B confuses a market price with a controlled price; D is a refusal to answer, not an outcome the market produces.
3. B: many sellers usually bring many varieties, stalls and service styles. A reverses the effect; C ignores the wider choice rivalry brings; D confuses a competitive market with a single standard product.
4. A: unusually high profit attracts new sellers, whose entry competes the margin down. B treats profit as protected, which describes a seller behind barriers, not a competitive one; C assumes buyers have no alternatives; D ignores the buyers who would switch away.
5. A: the single dominant seller behind barriers to entry is the definition. B confuses size with market structure - a large firm may still face many rivals; C confuses a monopoly with a market of a few sellers; D confuses a monopoly's own price-setting with a government-fixed price.
6. A: a licence is a legal barrier that keeps newcomers out. B names a feature of a competitive market; C names a shift in demand, which affects the market but keeps nobody out; D names a change in buyers' incomes, not an obstacle to entry.
7. B: the demand curve facing a dominant seller slopes downward, so a higher price tends to cost it sales. A reverses the direction of the demand curve; C confuses a movement along the curve with a shift of the curve; D confuses the seller's price with buyers' incomes.
8. A: where scale lowers cost per unit, part of the saving may reach buyers. B treats the absence of rivalry as an advantage to buyers rather than to the seller; C assumes the seller must extract the most, when it prices within what buyers will pay; D names a disadvantage, not an advantage.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and each distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Every distractor traces to a named error: a competitive market confused with a dominant seller's power, entry confused with exit, size confused with structure, a movement along the demand curve confused with a shift, and an advantage to the seller confused with an advantage to buyers.

items.prompt:
A newspaper report from Otavi, March 2027: "Otavi's bread now comes from a busier open market. Four bakeries traded at the market last year; seven trade this year, and the average loaf has fallen in price. The town's fuel comes from the single station at the crossroads, 80 km from the next forecourt."

Table 1 - Otavi markets
  bakeries trading last year: 4
  bakeries trading this year: 7
  average loaf price last year: N$15
  average loaf price this year: N$12
  crossroads station fuel price: N$25 a litre
  fuel price 80 km away: N$22 a litre

(a) Calculate the fall in the average loaf price between the two years. [1]
(b) Calculate how many more bakeries trade this year than last year. [1]
(c) Identify from Table 1 the fuel price households could find 80 km away. [2]
(d) Explain why the changes in the bread market show a competitive market working for buyers. [4]
(e) Analyse what the report suggests about the two markets for Otavi's households, using the data as evidence. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) N$15 - N$12 = N$3.
(b) 7 - 4 = 3 bakeries.
(c) N$22 a litre, at the station 80 km away.
(d) The changes show a competitive market at work: three new bakeries entered, so the number of sellers rose from four to seven; because buyers at the open market can switch freely between stalls, a dearer bakery tends to lose customers to a keener rival; this causes the average price to fall from N$15 to N$12 a loaf; and buyers gain both the N$3 lower price and the choice of seven stalls where four traded.
(e) The level of the price tends to track the number of sellers - many sellers with switching buyers tend towards lower prices, while a single protected seller tends towards higher ones - and the data fit this: bread fell N$3 a loaf as bakeries rose from four to seven, while the single station at the crossroads charges N$25 a litre against N$22 80 km away. In the bread market, the new sellers raise the quantity offered at each price and rivalry pulls the price down; in the fuel market, the distance to the next station is a barrier that keeps rivals out, so the station's price sits above the level households could find with a second station nearby. However, the fuel gap may partly reflect the transport cost of serving a remote crossroads, and the bread fall may owe something to a good flour season as well as to entry, so the data suggests rather than settles the two effects.
marking_guidance: Parts (a), (b) and (c) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the bakery numbers, the N$3 bread fall, the two fuel prices - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (d): the entry of new sellers, the switching of buyers, the falling price and the wider choice each need their link made.
Part (e) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for Otavi's households, the buyers of both goods.

facts: average loaf price last year N$15
average loaf price this year N$12
crossroads station fuel price N$25 a litre
fuel price 80 km away N$22 a litre

items.prompt:
A town council is reviewing its two markets. At the open market, twelve vegetable sellers trade, and new sellers may rent a stall on payment of a small weekly fee. The town's bus service is run by one licensed company, and the licence keeps other operators off the rank.

(a) Define a competitive market. [2]
(b) Explain two features of the town's bus market that make it a monopoly. [4]
(c) Analyse the effects on vegetable buyers and on the twelve existing sellers if three new sellers rent stalls. [6]
(d) Discuss whether the council should keep the bus market with its single licensed operator as it is. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A competitive market is a market with a high number of buyers and sellers in which each seller is too small to influence the market price on its own: the price is set by demand and supply across the whole market, and a seller who charges noticeably above it tends to lose customers to rivals.
(b) The first feature is a single dominant seller: one licensed company runs the buses, and in the extreme it is the town's only supplier of rank-based bus travel. Because it alone holds the licence, the fare is its own choice rather than the outcome of rivalry. The second feature is a barrier to entry: the licence is a legal barrier that keeps any other operator off the rank. Because newcomers cannot enter, the company keeps its position even where its fare sits above the level a second operator might charge.
(c) Three new sellers renting stalls raise the number of sellers from twelve to fifteen and the quantity of vegetables offered at each price. Because buyers can move freely between stalls and new sellers win trade by pricing keenly, the going price comes under downward pressure. For buyers, the price of vegetables tends to fall and the choice of stalls widens. Each of the twelve existing sellers faces a narrower margin as prices are pulled down, and a stall whose quality slips tends to lose buyers to a newcomer. The gains land on the buyers, and the squeezed margins on the existing sellers - the standard effect of entry into a market of many small sellers.
(d) Why the council might keep it: a single operator may run a steadier timetable across quiet routes, because it plans the whole network rather than choosing the busiest roads; and where its scale lowers its cost per trip, part of the saving may reach the fare. Why it might not: with the licence keeping rivals out, the fare may sit above the level a second operator would charge, and the pressure to keep the service good is weaker when passengers cannot easily switch. Judgement: on balance the council is likely to serve passengers better by keeping a single licensed network, provided the fare is checked against the operator's costs - the condition the judgement depends on is whether any check on the fare exists, since with the barrier in place the operator prices within what passengers will pay rather than near what rivalry would bring.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: many sellers, each too small to influence the price set across the market.
(b) one mark per distinct linked statement: each feature - the single licensed seller and the licence as a barrier - needs its consequence developed.
(c) one mark per distinct linked statement, from the starting point through the mechanism to the consequence for buyers and for the existing sellers.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - the steadier network and the scale saving that may reach the fare - and why it might not - the fare sitting above the rival level and the weaker pressure to keep quality up - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "A district with one dominant fuel supplier behind strong barriers to entry is considering opening its market to any licensed seller. Discuss whether households in the district are likely to gain." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (households gain):
Chain 1: barrier lifted -> new sellers enter -> the quantity offered at each price rises -> the price tends to fall towards the many-seller level (for whom: households buying fuel).
Chain 2: new sellers arrive -> rivalry for customers -> pressure on service and quality -> queues shorten and standards are held up (for whom: households).
Case against (households may gain little):
Chain 3: set-up costs in a scattered district are heavy -> entry stays thin, one or two sellers appear -> rivalry stays weak -> the price falls little (for whom: households).
Chain 4: the dominant seller meets entry by cutting its own price for a time -> newcomers withdraw -> the price drifts back towards its old level (for whom: households).
Judgement: households are likely to gain where entry is real - several sellers able to enter and stay - and the condition it depends on is whether the district's set-up costs let more than a token rival survive, because a market moves towards the many-seller level only where entry persists.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain ending on the group it lands on - households and the sellers who enter.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: whether the district's set-up costs let more than a token rival survive.
What settles it: whether entry persists - a market moves towards the many-seller level where several sellers can enter and stay.
